[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Oracle Triggers: DML, DDL, and System Triggers"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Triggers in Oracle databases are powerful PL/SQL blocks that automatically execute in response to specific events. These events can be data manipulation language (DML) operations, data definition language (DDL) statements, or system events. Triggers provide a mechanism to enforce business rules, audit data changes, and perform other tasks automatically."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"DML Triggers"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"DML triggers fire when a DML statement (INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE) affects a table or view. They can be defined to fire BEFORE or AFTER the triggering event, and FOR EACH ROW or FOR EACH STATEMENT."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"BEFORE triggers: Execute before the DML operation. Useful for validating data or modifying it before it's written to the database."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"AFTER triggers: Execute after the DML operation. Useful for auditing changes or performing actions based on the new data."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FOR EACH ROW triggers: Execute once for each row affected by the DML operation. Can access the old and new values of the row."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FOR EACH STATEMENT triggers: Execute once for the entire DML statement, regardless of the number of rows affected."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER audit_employee_changes
AFTER UPDATE ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO employee_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary, update_date)
  VALUES (:OLD.employee_id, :OLD.salary, :NEW.salary, SYSDATE);
END;"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the above example, the 'audit_employee_changes' trigger fires after an UPDATE statement on the 'employees' table. It's a FOR EACH ROW trigger, so it executes for every updated row. ':OLD' refers to the old value of a column before the update, and ':NEW' refers to the new value after the update. This trigger inserts a record into an 'employee_audit' table to track salary changes."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"DDL Triggers"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"DDL triggers fire in response to DDL statements, such as CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and RENAME. They are useful for auditing schema changes, enforcing naming conventions, or preventing unauthorized modifications to the database structure."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"DDL triggers can be defined at the DATABASE or SCHEMA level."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"They can be used to prevent certain DDL operations from being executed."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER prevent_table_drop
BEFORE DROP ON SCHEMA
BEGIN
  IF ora_dict_obj_type = 'TABLE' THEN
    RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001, 'Dropping tables is not allowed.');
  END IF;
END;"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"This DDL trigger, 'prevent_table_drop', fires before any DROP operation on the schema. It checks if the object being dropped is a table. If it is, the trigger raises an application error, preventing the DROP operation from succeeding. The 'ora_dict_obj_type' function returns the type of object being affected by the DDL statement."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"System Triggers"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"System triggers fire in response to database system events, such as STARTUP, SHUTDOWN, LOGON, and LOGOFF. They can be used for auditing user activity, enforcing security policies, or performing maintenance tasks."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"System triggers are defined at the DATABASE level."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"They can be used to track user login times or enforce password policies."},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER audit_logon
AFTER LOGON ON DATABASE
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO logon_audit (username, logon_time)
  VALUES (USER, SYSDATE);
END;"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'audit_logon' trigger fires after a user logs on to the database. It inserts a record into the 'logon_audit' table, recording the username and logon time. The 'USER' function returns the current username."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Considerations"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"When using triggers, consider the following:"},{"order":25,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Performance: Triggers can impact performance, especially FOR EACH ROW triggers. Optimize trigger logic to minimize overhead."},{"order":26,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Complexity: Overuse of triggers can make database logic difficult to understand and maintain. Document triggers clearly."},{"order":27,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cascading Triggers: Avoid creating triggers that trigger other triggers, as this can lead to unexpected behavior and infinite loops."},{"order":28,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Error Handling: Implement robust error handling within triggers to prevent them from failing silently."},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"By understanding the different types of triggers and their capabilities, you can effectively use them to enhance data integrity, enforce business rules, and automate database tasks in Oracle."}]
